finding.claim: DELETE /files/<fid> performs no authorization check: is_allowed (aliased require_allowed) returns a bool that is discarded, so delete proceeds for any caller including g.user=None.
finding.source: Any HTTP DELETE request to /files/<fid>; no identity or header required
finding.guards_checked: acl.ensure_allowed (aborts 403) is correct but not used on this route; is_allowed fails closed for None but its result gates nothing. Downgraded CRITICAL->HIGH: fid enumerability and external reachability not confirmed (triage Check 13 Q1, Q3). Validation tier 0.

verdict.guard_found: none. views.py:3-4 imports is_allowed as require_allowed, and views.py:18 calls it as a bare statement, so its bool return (acl.py:4-5) is discarded. The only other control is ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, aborts 403), which the delete route does not call. views.py:12 (before_request) only sets g.user from a header and enforces nothing. views.py:19 then runs del STORE[fid] unconditionally.
verdict.reason: views.py:18 discards the bool from require_allowed (acl.py:4 is_allowed), so views.py:19 deletes STORE[fid] for any caller, including g.user=None from views.py:12. The only attacker precondition is knowing a valid fid, which is a reachability condition rather than a guard; no file in the directory adds auth middleware.

finding.claim: Caller identity is taken from the unverified client header X-Session-User-Verified and trusted as the authenticated principal for grant checks.
finding.sink: g.user used by ensure_allowed at views.py:26 (rename, write grant) and require_allowed at views.py:18

trace.note: before_request load_user runs on every request
g.user copied from header without verification

finding.guards_checked: No signature, session lookup, or proxy-strip of the header in scope. .get(user, []) default fails closed only for absent/unknown identities. Would drop to LOW if an upstream proxy strips and re-injects the header (not visible in scope). Validation tier 0.

verdict.guard_found: None validate the identity. acl.py:8-10 ensure_allowed does abort(403) on failure, but it only checks grants for whatever user string it is given, so a spoofed name that holds a grant passes. views.py:18 require_allowed is a bare is_allowed call that returns a bool and discards it, so it is a no-op guard. views.py:12 has no signature, session, or strip check.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 copies the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header into g.user with no verification, and views.py:26 and acl.py:5 use that value directly for the grant lookup, so any unauthenticated HTTP client who names a user holding "write" can rename a file. The only caveat is that an upstream proxy stripping and re-injecting the header is not visible in this repo, which would lower severity but does not refute the in-scope flaw.

finding.claim: Object-existence oracle: unknown fid raises unhandled KeyError (500) while existing-but-denied objects return 403, letting unauthenticated callers enumerate valid IDs.
finding.sink: Differential response (500 vs 403) at views.py:25-26 and acl.py:10

trace.note: STORE[fid] raises KeyError for unknown id, no handler registered
abort(403) for existing object without grant

finding.guards_checked: No errorhandler for KeyError/404 registered. Bounded, non-actionable alone (Check 8); enables AUTH-1 ID-knowledge precondition. Retained at MEDIUM.

verdict.guard_found: None blocks the oracle. views.py:25 does a bare STORE[fid] lookup before any check, so an unknown id raises KeyError. The only error handling is acl.py:10 abort(403), reached only for existing objects. No errorhandler or 404 handler is registered anywhere in the directory (grep found none). load_user (views.py:10-12) only copies a request header and does not reject unauthenticated callers, so the route is reachable anonymously.
verdict.reason: The rename route at views.py:25-26 returns an unhandled 500 for unknown ids and acl.py:10 returns 403 for existing ids without a grant, and nothing between the anonymous caller and that branch blocks the difference, so the existence oracle is real. The candidate overgeneralizes: on the delete route (views.py:18) require_allowed is is_allowed, which returns a bool that is discarded, so an existing id is deleted with no 403 at all. That is a separate and more serious missing-authorization bug the candidate did not report.

finding.claim: Grant check uses the 'in' operator on the stored grant value; if a grant were a string, substring matches would authorize (e.g. 'write' in 'rewrite').
finding.source: Stored grants data shape (no producer in scope)

trace.note: membership test on whatever is stored for user

finding.guards_checked: No code in scope produces string grants; latent hazard only. LOW hardening, not counted in metrics.

verdict.guard_found: none needed: the only sink is acl.py:5, and the flaw requires grants to be stored as a string, which nothing in scope does. views.py:26 is the only caller and passes a fixed "write" action and the resource from the app, not attacker-controlled grant data.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (acl.py:5 is a membership test on whatever `grants[user]` holds), but the substring bypass needs a string-valued grant, and no code in scope writes grants at all (grep finds only the read at acl.py:5 and the call at views.py:26), so an attacker has no path to put a string there; this is a hypothetical latent hazard, not a reachable vulnerability.
